query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of Hf (~0.5 at%) to the eutectic high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of fine Hf‐rich precipitates along the lamellar colony interfaces, thereby strengthening these internal boundaries, retarding microcrack initiation, and ultimately simultaneously increasing both room‐temperature tensile strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional AlCoCrFeNi2.1-type eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting dual-phase (e.g., fcc/B2) lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that are prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, trace addition of Hf (around 0.5 at%) into the alloy composition during casting, followed by a standard thermo-mechanical processing schedule designed to develop and retain the eutectic lamellar structure.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing on standardized dog-bone specimens combined with microstructural characterization (using SEM, TEM, EBSD) to verify the distribution and size of the Hf-rich precipitates at the colony boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: Fine Hf-rich precipitates selectively precipitated along the internal lamellar (phase) boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The fine Hf-rich precipitates act as pinning agents at the internal boundaries, which enhances interfacial cohesion. By impeding the initiation and propagation of microcracks along these internal interfaces, the precipitates promote effective load transfer during deformation. This dual effect reinforces the strength while offering additional energy dissipation paths during tensile straining, thereby improving ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified alloy, the Hf-added alloy is predicted to exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths along with increased ductility (i.e., higher elongation to failure) at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with unmodified lamellar colony microstructures that display high strength yet limited room-temperature ductility due to microcrack initiation at internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only within a narrow Hf concentration window; excessive Hf could lead to large or continuous intermetallic phases that may embrittle the material. Moreover, the alloy must retain its characteristic lamellar microstructure during processing for the mechanism to be effective.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal Hf content and size/distribution of the precipitates that maximizes the balance between strength and ductility are uncertain and require further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of AlCoCrFeNi2.1-based alloys with Hf contents of 0, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at% using identical casting and thermo-mechanical processing routes to ensure retention of the eutectic lamellar structure. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and perform detailed microstructural analysis (SEM, TEM, EBSD) to assess precipitate formation at colony boundaries.
measurements: Room-temperature yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Distribution, size, and morphology of Hf-rich precipitates at the lamellar interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the trace Hf addition does not result in a statistically significant simultaneous improvement in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the baseline alloy, or if the addition leads to formation of coarse or continuous intermetallic phases that reduce ductility, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Developing alloys with ultrahigh strength and excellent ductility simultaneously over a wide temperature range is crucial for developing high-temperature steam turbines [,,]. Recently, as a category of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), dual-phase high-entropy alloys (DP-HEAs) with a soft FCC phase and hard BCC (B2) phase have been reported to have excellent strength–ductility synergy at ambient temperature and high temperature [,,,,,,,,,], and thus have great potential to be used as steam turbine hot end components. Unfortunately, due to the rapid softening of the phase with the BCC structure at high temperatures, the yield strength of the alloy will significantly decrease [,,,,,]. Moreover, due to the weakness of grain boundaries and phase boundaries, the cracks initiate rapidly and propagate along the interface during high-temperature deformation, severely limiting the high-temperature application of FCC/B2 dual-phase high-entropy alloys [,,,,].

As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.
